cells.tense: How much goes out and when is your call right now, and you're making it from the ground.
cells.ask: Pick one person and tell them, in plain words, what you're keeping alive and what it takes from you each week. Saying it out loud lets you stand next to it instead of under it.
cells.core:
On a good day here you add a little where it's wanted and hold steady where it isn't, and the adjusting doesn't eat the rest of your evening. You keep something going and still have something left at the end of the day.

Today the readjusting runs all day and the quiet at the end doesn't arrive, because nothing you're carrying has reached a point where you can stop touching it. Pick one person and tell them, in plain words, what you're keeping alive and what it takes from you each week. Said out loud, the hours you spend on it take up room they didn't before.

cells.tense: You're living in the season that hasn't come yet, and the thing in front of you is going unfed.
cells.ask: Give the thing that's actually in front of you one plain act of care today — fifteen minutes, nothing past the act. Doing it puts you back in contact with the ground your plan is standing on.
cells.core:
On a good day here the making and the keeping-up take turns. You give what's in front of you what it needs, stop when it's satisfied, and let the fruit come when it comes.

Right now your head is at a harvest that's still ahead of you, so the thing in your hands gets what's left over. Give that one thing one plain act of care today — fifteen minutes, nothing past the act. cells.tense: You set something down and you're still where you left it, past the point where you could have picked it back up.
cells.ask: Put one line on paper today about what you'd tend if you began again, and leave it where tomorrow's you will see it. A first step you can see makes the way back a step, not a door.
cells.core:
On a good day here you reach for it again without needing to explain, undo, or make up for the gap. The care hasn't gone anywhere, and it can start from where it actually stopped.

What's absent at the moment isn't appetite for it — the first step hasn't happened yet, so beginning again reads as a door to walk back through. Put one line on paper today about what you'd tend if you began again, and leave it where tomorrow's you will see it. What comes off that isn't polish. It's heat from work that actually went somewhere.

cells.tense: Your hands are in this work, and the way the story comes out of your mouth, those hands belong to someone else.
cells.ask: Say the plain sentence out loud once, to yourself or to someone who knows the work — this got kept going because someone decided what to feed and when. Hearing it said gives a finished thing back to the one who finished it.
cells.core:
On a good day here you say what you did and how it held, and the saying sits next to the doing without fuss. You check what's low, you feed what needs it, you steady what's tall, and then you can describe that as yours.

The describing is the part that's missing. The work happens; the saying about it doesn't, and what comes out of your mouth sounds like the day arrived on its own. Say the plain sentence out loud once, to yourself or to someone who knows the work — this got kept going because someone decided what to feed and when. The sentence adds no weight. Hearing it is what lets you set a finished thing down, because you can hear whose it was.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is holding two growing things at once — the draw says two demands kept in balance, and I don't know their life, so every cell points at what's visible in front of them and lets them decide it names their situation. The likely objection is 'I'm not tending any living thing' — a reasonable reader says the card isn't about their plants or kids, so the ask never names the thing: they choose it, and telling one person about the thing they're actually tending is still useful even if I've guessed the subject wrong. The sentence that serves the writer is 'Two things, both being watered' — it puts the whole picture in one image and sounds like the house, so I'm cutting the image entirely and letting the two-pails sentence do the work.
